parts.spoken_English: On Spitsbergen, in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, a corridor has been drilled deep into a frosted hillside.
At its end, cartons of precious seed sit silently in a sub-zero repository, insulated by permanently frozen ground.
The Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened near Longyearbyen in February 2008 to insure crops such as beans, rice, and wheat against the horrors people dread, from atomic war to disease.
It has ample room for about four and a half million samples.
Essentially the planet's ultimate backup, it is run like a bank's safe-deposit box.
Depositors keep ownership, and only they can take their seeds out.
The first retrieval came not after an asteroid strike but amid strife on the ground.
ICARDA, a research centre whose gene bank stood near Aleppo, had moved its headquarters to Beirut during Syria's civil war.
In September 2015 it asked for about 116,000 samples, 130 of the 325 boxes it had sent to the Arctic before the hostilities.
They included robust strains of wheat and barley tolerant of drought and heat.
In Lebanon and Morocco, ICARDA sowed the seeds, and vigorous plants sprouted to regenerate its collection.
Once multiplication had gone far enough, a homecoming began in 2017, consignment by consignment, restocking the Arctic stronghold.
That same year brought a scare.
After record-breaking warmth, meltwater ran into the roughly 100-metre entrance tunnel and solidified.
The intrusion stopped short of the seeds, which stayed safely at minus 18 degrees Celsius.
Norway waterproofed the tunnel and dug drainage ditches.
A haven built against the apocalypse had a weakness at its own entrance, and warmer weather found it.
